conflict_topics: Stove access / scheduling (who can cook when)
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants speak like roommates with concise, situational claims (e.g., C: 'someone needs to wash it').
Positions are restated rather than developed into options or proposals (some repetition of stove-access and washing claims).
No confusion about roles or facts; the physical setting and constraints remain consistent throughout.
evaluation.final_reason: No substantive agreement was reached. Multiple incompatible issues (who washes the shared pan, how to manage stove access/times, and the smell problem) were raised and defended (e.g., Agent A arguing entitlement because they buy supplies, Agents C/D insisting buying supplies doesn't excuse not washing). No party accepted another's proposal and no concrete mutual arrangement was agreed in the transcript.
position_change_notes: No participant changed position during the run: A maintained that they need to cook and asserted entitlement from buying supplies; C and D maintained that someone must wash the pan and rejected entitlement as an excuse; B emphasized smell but did not propose a compromise.
Positions were reinforced by repetition and counterstatements rather than negotiated concessions.

round_scores.evidence: Turn 1 (Agent C): '...This pan is still here from last night.' Turn 2 (Agent D): '...I still need to cook though, and it's always impossible to get on the stove this late.' -- Two substantive problems (unwashed shared pan; stove access) are raised and are incompatible interests.

Turn 3 (Agent A): 'Whose pan is it anyway?' Turn 4 (Agent C): 'Doesn't matter whose it is. Someone needs to wash it.' -- The complaint about the unwashed pan is reiterated and the demand for someone to clean it remains unresolved.

Turn 5 (Agent D): '...we still have to figure out the stove access. It's always a problem for me when I get back late.' Turn 6 (Agent A): 'I cook most nights because it's the only break I get after working from home all day.' -- Directly competing claims over stove priority/times create a clearer substantive disagreement.

Turn 7 (Agent B): 'The smell is the problem, not when you cook.' Turn 8 (Agent C): 'Yeah, the smell is bad too.' -- A related but distinct substantive issue (cooking smell affecting others) is added; no settlement.

Turn 9 (Agent D): '...I also need to cook when I get home. It's tough when the stove is always taken.' Turn 10 (Agent A): '...I'm the one who buys all the dish soap and gas for the stove, so I use it.' -- Agent A asserts an entitlement-based justification for continued use; others' access needs remain in direct conflict.

Turn 12 (Agent C): 'Buying soap doesn't mean you don't have to wash up.' Turn 13 (Agent D): 'Buying stuff for the flat doesn't mean you get to skip washing up.' -- Other agents explicitly reject Agent A's entitlement argument; the dispute over washing, responsibility, smell, and stove access remains unresolved.

substantive_insights: Tension is partly between contribution (buying dish soap/gas) and reciprocal chores: A treats contribution as entitlement, others treat it as insufficient to avoid cleaning.
Temporal access needs conflict: one person cooks most nights for personal break, another needs to cook after returning late—there is no schedule or agreed priority.
The smell issue links to both washing practices (dirty pan) and cooking timing; addressing one problem (washing) might reduce smell but not resolve stove scheduling.
